revisions.title: Testing pleasure’s claim to truth
revisions.body: This section turns pleasure into a test of appearances. Future hopes are pictured in the soul, yet pleasures and pains can look larger or smaller when set beside one another. The inquiry also considers the view that pleasures are escapes from pain, asking us to compare these accounts rather than treat immediacy as proof.

revisions.title: Intensity Is Not Yet Value
revisions.body: Here the inquiry tests intensity at its extremes, looking to sickness rather than health; it then widens to mixtures in body, soul, and both. By the end, laughter at a friend’s ridiculousness is traced through envy to a pleasure that carries pain. Intensity, on this reading, is evidence to examine, not a verdict of value.

Socrates tests the leap from one shared name to one shared value. Protarchus grants that pleasures arise from opposed conditions, while Socrates answers with the color-and-shape analogy and asks what identical element could make unlike pleasures all good. Protarchus deflects the demand rather than resolving it, leaving the claim that pleasure is the good under pressure.
